Inquiry means the act of seeking information or truth. Whenever someone tries to find something out — by asking a question, investigating a situation, or examining facts carefully — that process is an inquiry. Think of it as any deliberate effort to move from not knowing to knowing.
The Two Main Meanings

The word "inquiry" works in two closely related but distinct ways:

1. A question, or the act of asking one

In everyday use, an inquiry is simply a question asked to obtain information. It implies you don't have the answer yet, and you're reaching out to find it.

"She made an inquiry about the bus schedule."
"The company received several inquiries about the job posting."
"He called the bank to make an inquiry about his account."

Notice: you don't just "say" an inquiry — you make one. The word suggests a purposeful, directed act, not idle chat.

2. A formal, official investigation

In a more serious and structured context, an inquiry is an organized process of examining facts, usually carried out by an authority, institution, or group of experts, in order to find the truth about something — especially something that went wrong, is unclear, or is disputed.

"The government launched a public inquiry into the train crash."
"A judicial inquiry was set up to look into the allegations of corruption."
"The committee's inquiry took six months and interviewed dozens of witnesses."

This kind of inquiry is much bigger than a single question. It has a purpose, a structure, and usually produces a report or conclusion at the end.
How the Two Meanings Connect

Both meanings share the same essential DNA: actively seeking truth or information. The difference is only in scale and formality:

← CasualFormal →
A customer asking a shop if a product is in stockA government investigating why a dam collapsed

Both are "inquiries." One is a moment; the other is a months-long process. The word fits both.
Important Nuance: Inquiry vs. a Simple Question

Not every question is an inquiry. The word carries a slight sense of seriousness and purpose. You wouldn't normally say "I made an inquiry about what's for dinner." That's too trivial. Inquiry fits when:

  • You are genuinely seeking factual information.
  • There is some effort or deliberateness involved.
  • The matter has some weight or consequence.

So "inquiry" sits between a casual question and a full investigation — though it can stretch to mean either, depending on context.
The Phrase "A Line of Inquiry"

You'll often see "inquiry" used in the phrase a line of inquiry. This means a particular direction or angle of questioning or investigation that someone is following in order to uncover the truth.

"The detective pursued several lines of inquiry before identifying the suspect."
"The researchers opened a new line of inquiry into the causes of the disease."

Think of it like a thread you pull to see where it leads.
"Inquiry Into" — A Key Pattern

The word is very commonly followed by "into" when referring to an investigation:

"an inquiry into the cause of the explosion"
"an inquiry into government spending"
"an inquiry into the matter"

This "into" signals that you are looking inside something — digging beneath the surface to understand it.
Spelling Note: "Inquiry" vs. "Enquiry"

You will sometimes see the spelling enquiry (with an e). Both words mean the same thing. The difference is largely regional:

  • Inquiry is the standard spelling in American English and is used for both meanings.
  • In British English, some writers prefer enquiry for the casual meaning (asking a question) and inquiry for the formal, official investigation — but this distinction is not strictly followed by everyone, and both spellings are widely accepted in either sense.

Unless you're writing for a specific British audience, you can safely use inquiry in all situations.
Synonyms to Anchor Your Understanding

To lock the meaning in your mind, here are words that overlap with "inquiry" depending on context:

  • Question / Query — when the inquiry is just asking something
  • Investigation — when it's a serious, structured inquiry
  • Examination / Review — when something is being carefully looked into
  • Probe — a pointed or penetrating inquiry, often into wrongdoing
  • Inquest — a very specific type of formal inquiry, usually into a death
  • Research — a broad, ongoing process of inquiry, especially in academics or science
"Inquiry" in Intellectual and Scientific Life

Beyond questions and official investigations, "inquiry" has a powerful place in education, philosophy, and science. Scientific inquiry refers to the entire process by which scientists observe, question, hypothesize, test, and draw conclusions. Philosophical inquiry refers to deep, reasoned examination of fundamental questions about life, knowledge, and existence.

In this sense, inquiry is seen as one of the highest human activities — the engine of knowledge itself.

"The spirit of inquiry has driven human progress for centuries."
"Good education should foster a love of inquiry in students."

Here, "inquiry" is almost a virtue — the habit of not accepting things blindly but asking why and how until you truly understand.
Summary

Inquiry (noun) means:

  1. A question or act of asking — to get information you don't yet have.
  2. A formal investigation — an organized, serious effort to find the truth about something.

At every level — from asking a hotel about its check-in time to a government examining a national crisis — "inquiry" captures the act of deliberately seeking to know. It is always purposeful, always directed at something specific, and always motivated by the desire to move from uncertainty toward understanding.
